articles.title_orig: No choice made yet by Trump on resuming military action against Iran, Rubio says
articles.title_zh: No choice made yet by Trump on resuming military action against Iran, Rubio says
articles.content_orig:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump "hasn't made a decision" whether or not to resume strikes on Iran.
Rubio, speaking at the G20 meeting in Atlanta, said Trump prefers to solve the conflict diplomatically.
"This is also a country and a regime that is at the center of all the instability in the Middle East," Rubio said earlier. "In Lebanon there is instability because they support Hezbollah. In Saudi Arabia they are under attack because Iran supports the Houthis. In Iraq, is a country that is feeling challenged because Iranian-backed militias are challenging the state there. So anywhere you turn what you find is some Iranian proxy that's undermining the peace and stability of the Middle East. That is a fundamental threat that we have to confront, on top of the fact that they want nuclear weapons."
"This is a regime that has massacred its own people," he added. "You could only imagine what it would do to others if it possessed weapons of mass destruction, which will never be allowed to happen as long as President Trump is in the White House."
Fox News contributor and former CIA station chief Dan Hoffman warned Saturday that Iran may be seeking a prolonged conflict with the U.S. despite mounting economic pressure and diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Speaking on "Fox Report," Hoffman said Tehran has shown little willingness to negotiate on Washington's terms, pointing to recent outreach involving Vice President JD Vance, Qatari mediators and regional officials.
"There's no indication that they feel like this war is a loser for them," Hoffman said.
Hoffman argued that Iran's leadership appears willing to withstand economic hardship while attempting to weaken the U.S. military presence in the Middle East.
He also warned that renewed American strikes could trigger Iranian retaliation against U.S. military bases and critical energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.
Hoffman said Iran retains ballistic missiles, drones and other capabilities that could be used in retaliatory attacks, adding that the Trump administration would need to prepare for those risks before resuming military operations.
Fox News senior strategic analyst retired Gen. Jack Keane expressed skepticism Saturday about the prospects of a diplomatic agreement with Iran amid reports that Vice President JD Vance contacted an Iranian hard-liner at President Donald Trump's direction.
Speaking on "Saturday in America," Keane argued that months of diplomatic efforts have demonstrated that Tehran is unwilling to negotiate a meaningful agreement.
"What have we learned in six and a half months of a diplomatic effort with the Iranians?" he said. "We learned that one thing they really not serious about making a consequential deal. And two, overwhelmingly everybody in the region knows. And I think most people in the United States, frankly, know, even if you're paying half attention to this issue, is that they would never comply with it."
Keane's remarks come as Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Trump has not decided whether to resume military strikes against Iran but prefers a diplomatic resolution.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that a proposal discussed with mediators could allow the Strait of Hormuz to fully reopen within two days, according to The Associated Press .
The development comes as Iranian negotiators hold talks with Qatari mediators in Doha aimed at ending the war with the U.S.
Araghchi said Tehran has no immediate plans to meet directly with American officials, despite ongoing diplomatic efforts.
Iran previously offered to reopen the strategic waterway within a week if Washington agreed to several demands, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, releasing frozen Iranian assets and easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, AP reported.
The U.S. rejected that earlier proposal, according to the news agency.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump has not decided whether to resume strikes against Iran, but prefers a diplomatic resolution.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Saturday that Tehran remains open to diplomacy if its seven conditions are met, while threatening military retaliation if the country comes under attack.
"We have repeatedly stated; the seven conditions announced by Iran must be fulfilled. If the conditions are met, the path of diplomacy will be open," Rezaei wrote on X.
"In response, if any action is taken against the country, in accordance with the Supreme Leader's directive today to the armed forces, we will deliver devastating blows to the aggressor using new weaponry," he added.
Rezaei's comments came after Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei instructed the country's armed forces Saturday to prepare for a response to threats without geographic restrictions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said Saturday that President Donald Trump has not decided whether to resume strikes against Iran, but prefers a diplomatic resolution.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Saturday that shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has returned to near prewar levels, excluding Iranian oil shipments.
"The Strait of Hormuz transit levels are back to pre-conflict levels minus Iranian barrels," Bessent wrote on X.
"The world can live without Iranian oil," he added. "Iran cannot live without oil exports."
Bessent also shared a graphic labeled "Operation Economic Outcast" showing 1.5 billion barrels of oil exported through the Strait of Hormuz by the U.S. and zero barrels by Iran.
The remarks come as the U.S. continues its blockade of Iranian ports amid the ongoing war with Tehran.
U.S. Central Command ( CENTCOM ) released a photo Saturday showing a U.S. sailor signaling to an F/A-18 Super Hornet fighter jet during nighttime operations aboard the USS George H.W. Bush aircraft carrier.
The image, shared on CENTCOM's official X account, shows the sailor holding illuminated signaling wands on the carrier's flight deck as the fighter jet prepares to maneuver.
The USS George H.W. Bush has been operating in the Middle East in support of the U.S. military's blockade of Iranian ports amid the ongoing war with Iran.
Strikes launched by Iran against more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East have resulted in billions of dollars of equipment damage, according to The Associated Press.
The news agency cited its analysis on satellite imagery from multiple providers and said it spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit.
The AP reported that through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with American equipment. Many of the attacks focused on aircraft hangars and systems that detect incoming strikes, the AP added.
It said most of the Iranian attacks have been in Kuwait, but U.S. sites in Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates also have been targeted.
Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait was struck at least 30 times, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to the AP.
This satellite image taken over Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait on July 24, 2026, shows the result of numerous strikes on this section of the bas. (Airbus DS 2026 via AP)
Al Dhafra Air Base, about 20 miles south of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates, was hit frequently early in the war, a regional military official with direct knowledge of the damage told the AP. The official noted damage to infrastructure like aircraft hangars and other installations as well as to equipment such as an early-warning radar system and surveillance drones.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon for comment.

articles.title_orig: G20 foreign ministers end Atlanta meeting without consensus on key issues
articles.title_zh: G20 foreign ministers end Atlanta meeting without consensus on key issues
articles.content_orig:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

articles.title_orig: China makes early progress in using sound waves to stimulate damaged brains
articles.title_zh: China makes early progress in using sound waves to stimulate damaged brains
articles.content_orig:
The technique uses magnetic resonance imaging to identify specific areas of the brain for stimulation, particularly the thalamus.
This structure acts as a central relay between different neural networks and plays an important role in consciousness, sensory processing and communication across the brain.
The approach is based on the idea that stimulating disrupted neural networks could help restore some of the activity associated with conscious behaviour.
Chinese researchers are testing whether focused ultrasound can help restore consciousness in patients with severe brain injuries, adding to a growing international effort to use sound waves to stimulate deep brain structures without surgery.
A team involving the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology has used targeted ultrasound pulses to stimulate brain regions associated with awareness and communication. The technology was presented at a brain-computer interface industry conference in Shenzhen, where researchers highlighted a potential medical application beyond the field’s better-known efforts to connect brains with computers and robotic systems.
According to Chinese state media, one patient who had spent three months in a coma after a brain haemorrhage regained the ability to speak, eat independently and walk with assistance following a month of ultrasound treatment and rehabilitation.
The technique uses magnetic resonance imaging to identify specific areas of the brain for stimulation, particularly the thalamus. This structure acts as a central relay between different neural networks and plays an important role in consciousness, sensory processing and communication across the brain .
Researchers then direct focused ultrasound pulses towards the selected regions. Unlike conventional approaches involving implanted electrodes or invasive surgery, the method is designed to reach deep brain structures from outside the skull.
The approach is based on the idea that stimulating disrupted neural networks could help restore some of the activity associated with conscious behaviour. This is particularly relevant to patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness, including those who remain in minimally conscious or vegetative states following traumatic injuries, strokes or other neurological events.
In a preliminary study conducted with Kunming Medical University, 24 patients with chronic disorders of consciousness received three 20-minute ultrasound sessions per week over four weeks. Chinese media reported that 13 of them showed improvements in conscious behaviour.
The results follow a peer-reviewed case study published by the same research group in Frontiers in Psychiatry in February. The paper tracked one patient treated with focused ultrasound and documented progressive behavioural improvements, with the patient eventually emerging from a minimally conscious state.
Researchers in the US are pursuing a more extensive clinical assessment. A multicentre trial led by the University of California, Los Angeles, is recruiting 60 patients with severe brain injuries. It includes a sham-stimulation control group, allowing investigators to compare patients receiving actual ultrasound treatment with those undergoing a simulated procedure.
Focused ultrasound is attracting attention because it can influence brain activity without requiring implanted hardware. That makes it a potential tool for neurological research and treatment, although questions remain about the optimal stimulation parameters, patient selection, treatment duration and long-term effects.
The development also signals a broader effort to create less invasive ways of interacting with the brain. While some BCI projects focus on translating neural signals into commands for computers or robotic devices, ultrasound-based approaches could potentially stimulate neural activity or enable new forms of communication with brain tissue.
Bojan Stojkovski is a freelance journalist based in Skopje, North Macedonia, covering foreign policy and technology for more than a decade. His work has appeared in Foreign Policy, ZDNet, and Nature.

articles.title_orig: Eisenkot sets conditions for coalition, vows to use Knesset majority to reverse Netanyahu policies
articles.title_zh: Eisenkot sets conditions for coalition, vows to use Knesset majority to reverse Netanyahu policies
articles.content_orig:
Yashar chairman Gadi Eisenkot laid out four principles for joining his proposed coalition on Saturday, saying that “any MK” willing to accept them could become a partner in forming the next government.
Election Day results saw Yashar win 21 seats in the Knesset, with the Eisenkot bloc at 48 total; the Likud won 27 seats, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc at 53 overall; and the Arab parties won 19 seats.
After the completion of the vote count, Eisenkot said he intended to establish the broadest possible Zionist, statesmanlike government, bringing together elected representatives who agree on Israel’s fundamental character, national service obligations, and the need to eliminate Hamas’s military and governing capabilities in the Gaza Strip.
“Any MK willing to sign on to these principles is a potential partner in establishing a new government that will be good for Israel,” Eisenkot said. “The door to the government we establish will be open to any elected official who accepts these principles and is prepared to rise to the occasion.”
Eisenkot’s conditions for any prospective coalition partner are: The recognition of Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal, and egalitarian state; a commitment to the values of the Declaration of Independence; mandatory military, national, or civilian service for all Israeli citizens; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization and acknowledgment of the obligation to destroy its military and governing power in the Gaza Strip.
Eisenkot said the principles would serve as the foundation for a broad government based on national consensus, rather than one seeking to impose the will of one political camp on another.
This latest development came amid a demonstration in Tel Aviv calling for a government of Arab and Jewish parties.
During the election campaign, Eisenkot pledged to establish a government capable of healing divisions and fundamentally changing Israel’s direction.
“I promised to reconnect Israel and put an end to the culture of lies led by Netanyahu that has torn us apart from within,” Eisenkot said. “I promised that under my leadership, one side would not defeat the other, and that the era of ‘us’ and ‘them’ was over.”
He said he would continue pursuing those commitments in the coming weeks while coordinating with his political partners to broaden the potential coalition.
“Based on these principles, I intend to establish the broadest possible Zionist, statesmanlike government,” Eisenkot said, adding that he aimed to fulfill the voters’ wishes and immediately improve Israel’s domestic and international standing.
Meanwhile, Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman denied reports that he was interested in becoming Knesset speaker in a post on X/Twitter on Saturday.
“The wicked never rest. I have received several inquiries regarding demands for the position of Knesset speaker. I have no desire and no intention of becoming Knesset speaker,” he wrote.

articles.title_orig: China expands, diversifies space launch infrastructure
articles.title_zh: China expands, diversifies space launch infrastructure
articles.content_orig:
TEHRAN, Oct. 31 (MNA) – China is expanding and diversifying its launch infrastructure to meet the growing demand from the commercial space industry, with its offshore launch platforms, commercial spaceports and dedicated launch pads etc.
A typical example is a commercial rocket carrying nine satellites that lifted off from a ship in the East China Sea near Shanghai in September this year. Although the densely populated economic hub has no traditional rocket launch site, sea-based launches are able to connect Shanghai to the country's growing space industry.
China's first sea launch took place in 2019, off the coast of Haiyang in east China's Shandong Province. The coastal city has since built a spaceport for rocket assembly, testing and launch operations. Teng Yao, chief engineer of the spaceport, said sea launches offer greater flexibility in choosing launch locations and trajectories, and allow rocket debris to fall into waters that are unpopulated.
Wenchang in south China's Hainan Province, which hosts a launch site tasked with missions of launching space station modules and lunar probes, has added facilities specifically for commercial rocket and satellite launches since 2024.
Meanwhile, the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone near the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China has developed launch pads tailored to private rocket makers.
Access to launch pads has been a challenge for China's commercial space sector. Wang Lifeng, a professor at Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, cited limited launch capacity, tight schedules and long distances between launch sites and rocket assembly facilities as constraints on growth.
Large satellite networks like Qianfan (or Spacesail) and GW constellations, which each have more than 10,000 satellites, further increase the need for a steady flow of launches.
Diversified facilities not only boost launch numbers but also make launch operations more efficient.
Wenchang's commercial spacecraft launch site has put its first two pads into regular service. The second pad alone can accommodate more than 20 rocket types and can be prepared for another launch in 66 hours. The third and fourth pads in the second phase are scheduled to be operational by the end of the year. Upon full commissioning, the site is able to handle about 60 launches annually.
Haiyang offers another route to greater efficiency. Peng Haomin, co-founder of Orienspace, said the private company's facilities are clustered in Haiyang's spaceport, allowing rockets to be assembled, tested and loaded onto a launch ship within 5 km.
"This has replaced usual transportation over more than 1,000 km, drastically cutting logistics time and cost," Peng said.
Dedicated facilities can also streamline rocket operations. Meng Xiangfu, deputy chief commander of Lijian-1 rocket of commercial spaceflight company CAS Space, said that with its tailored launch pad and technical facilities at the Dongfeng commercial space innovation pilot zone, the company can complete the testing and preparation of a rocket in 10 days.
The expansion of launch infrastructure not only benefits the space industry, but also helps boost local economy through investment.
With more than 30 aerospace projects landed, Haiyang has attracted 33.5 billion yuan (around 5 billion U.S. dollars) in related investment. Wenchang's space industry park hosts over 700 companies, while Shanghai is developing a commercial spaceport-related terminal to link rocket assembly with port logistics and sea launch services.
These developments fit into a broader global trend of investing in space capabilities to support the sector's growth, as the United States aims at expanding its space transportation capabilities and Russia calls for efforts to upgrade its industrial and ground-based space infrastructure.
A 2025-2027 action plan issued by the China National Space Administration calls for coordinated development of commercial space launch sites and supports new types of commercial launch systems, including sea-based launch and recovery facilities.
At the same time, China is pressing ahead with the development of heavy-lift and reusable launch vehicles to further expand launch capacity and improve cost efficiency.
Analysts note that efficient operation of these facilities could equip China's commercial space sector with the launch capacity and operational flexibility it needs.

articles.title_orig: Xona Is in Orbit. Its CEO Says U.S. GPS Backup Leans on China.
articles.title_zh: Xona Is in Orbit. Its CEO Says U.S. GPS Backup Leans on China.
articles.content_orig:
By Nick David, Editorial Lead, SatNews
Xona Space Systems put its first six commercial navigation satellites in orbit last week. On Thursday, its CEO laid out why the U.S. needs them: the backup most commercial users rely on today comes from China.
“We actually just launched our first six satellites last week that are going to start providing commercial service early next year,” Xona co-founder and CEO Brian Manning said on the MilSat Symposium panel “GPS Under Attack: Jamming, Spoofing, and the PNT Fight” at Silicon Valley Space Week, moderated by Ahsun Murad of Optimal Satcom. The Pulsar satellites flew Oct. 20 on SpaceX’s Bandwagon-5 rideshare, and Xona has said beta service begins in early 2027. The company closed a $250 million Series D two days after launch.
Manning said the problem is already showing up in drones built by the hundreds of thousands. Drone companies on the military side “are cutting the cable on the GPS chip because they don’t trust it,” he said. “It’s actually worse to have bad location than no location.” Jamming can be worked around with inertial sensors, but bad location “means you’re going to hit your own troops.”
Those builders don’t have access to M-code or other secure signals, Manning said, while faking GPS signals takes about as much skill as “typing the Google.”
Commercial users trying to make positioning more resilient mostly move to multi-constellation receivers, Manning said, and the newest constellation beyond GPS is China’s. U.S. industries from critical infrastructure timing to agriculture to logistics now integrate Chinese signals alongside GPS, “a vulnerability that has been ingrained into pretty much every single aspect of U.S. critical infrastructure,” he said.
Receiver makers can’t simply drop those signals and stay competitive globally, he acknowledged. “But right now relying on Chinese, Russian, et cetera, signals to get resilience does not put the U.S., I don’t think, in a very strong position.”
Col. Jon Strizzi, director of Space Systems Command’s Space Systems Integration Office, gave the Space Force’s GPS update. He said 14 GPS IIIF satellites, the next block, are on contract, with five moving through assembly, integration and test and first deliveries expected in mid-2027.
The panel also included Jeff Janicik, founder and chairman of Innoflight; Monali Jain, founder and CEO of AutonomousLabs.Space; and Sumant Sharma, co-founder and CEO of EraDrive.
Xona’s pitch is that commercial signals from low Earth orbit, roughly 20 times closer to Earth than GPS, can add the precision, power and protection that today’s receivers lack while plugging into the billions of GPS devices already in use.
A storyteller at heart, Nick David covers space policy, satellite markets, defense, and the technologies reshaping how humanity operates beyond Earth. With a background in creative direction, brand strategy, and editorial storytelling, he brings a modern lens to complex subjects and a relentless curiosity about what comes next.
Satnews is a leading provider of satellite news, events, publications, research and other satellite industry information in both commercial and military enterprises worldwide.

articles.title_orig: American chip billionaire Jensen Huang's Nvidia defends his meetings with suspected Chinese spy
articles.title_zh: American chip billionaire Jensen Huang's Nvidia defends his meetings with suspected Chinese spy
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia says billionaire CEO Jensen Huang did nothing unusual in meeting a Chinese executive whom U.S. intelligence officials concluded was gathering information for Beijing.
Nvidia Corp. has defended its billionaire chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, after a report that U.S. intelligence officials concluded a Chinese businesswoman who built a close relationship with him was gathering information for Beijing, and that President Donald Trump was told about it roughly a year ago but did not act.
The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese national and a former senior executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that buys Nvidia's artificial intelligence chips and rents out computing power, including to Chinese companies. She has not been charged with any crime, and neither has Megaspeed. U.S. officials did not believe Jensen Huang knew she was collecting information for China, according to people familiar with the classified intelligence. No one has accused him of wrongdoing.
Nvidia said the contacts were routine. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected," Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said. "Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.'s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." The company said customers such as Megaspeed receive ordinary business information, not trade secrets or anything tied to national security, and that it was confident the government would tell it if it believed someone was a threat to American industry.
Huang, 63, called Nvidia's business with Megaspeed normal on Oct. 29 and said the company had checked how the cloud provider used its chips. "We've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one," he said. He added that Alice Huang no longer works at Megaspeed.
U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang turned up her contacts with Jensen Huang and led officials to conclude she was passing information to Beijing, according to people familiar with the intelligence. Officials worried she could gain access to sensitive Nvidia technology or insight into Trump's thinking on chip exports to China. The two were photographed together at a bar in Taipei in June 2024 and were seen at a business dinner in May 2025.
Trump was briefed on the findings about a year ago. The administration took no action, and Jensen Huang never received a defensive briefing, the warning U.S. agencies sometimes give Americans who are being targeted by a foreign intelligence service. The White House, the CIA and the National Security Agency declined to comment.
Alice Huang did not respond to requests for comment. Megaspeed said it takes the matter seriously, has hired outside lawyers to run an internal investigation and has told U.S. authorities it will cooperate. China rejected the report. Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun called it "baseless and purely slanderous," and the Chinese Embassy in Washington described U.S. accusations as "groundless smears and slanders."
Megaspeed under investigation
The U.S. began looking at Megaspeed in late 2024, when a Commerce Department official visiting its data center in Malaysia found Nvidia equipment still sitting in boxes. Investigators suspected some of its chips were reaching China in breach of U.S. export rules, which bar the sale of Nvidia's most advanced processors there. A Malaysian sister company of Megaspeed bought at least $4.8 billion of AI equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records. Singapore authorities questioned Alice Huang in 2025 and released her.
Senator Tom Cotton asked the Commerce Department in October 2025 to investigate Megaspeed, and the Justice Department took over the case this year. Nvidia said earlier claims that Megaspeed helped Chinese buyers evade U.S. restrictions "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year." Megaspeed remains a listed Nvidia cloud partner.
The report lands at a sensitive time for Huang, who has become one of Trump's closest business allies. He persuaded the president to allow some chip sales to China in exchange for the U.S. government taking a share of the revenue, and he was a guest at the White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping in September. Trump personally owns Nvidia shares.
Born in Taiwan, Huang moved to the U.S. as a child and co-founded Nvidia in 1993. He has run the company ever since, turning a maker of graphics cards for video games into the dominant supplier of the chips used to build AI systems. His stake in Nvidia has made him one of the richest people in the world.

articles.title_orig: Poland's president accuses Tusk of forced takeover of country's top court
articles.title_zh: Poland's president accuses Tusk of forced takeover of country's top court
articles.content_orig:
Prime Minister Donald Tusk addressed Poland’s deepening Constitutional Tribunal crisis in a televised speech on Saturday evening, vowing that the rule of law would prevail over violence as tensions over the country's judiciary reach boiling point.
The dispute over the composition of Poland’s top court has fuelled an open confrontation with President Karol Nawrocki, who attempted to enter the Tribunal building amid a deadlock over the appointment of new judges on Friday night.
Police surrounded the building as the confrontation unfolded live on television, drawing attention to the crisis beyond Poland and into the wider European political debate.
The opposition has accused Tusk’s government of attempting a coup, while the government says it is pushing ahead with long-needed reforms to restore the rule of law after years of PiS interference in the judiciary.
In his address to the nation, Tusk described Friday’s events as “scandalous incidents” and said he hoped such scenes would never be repeated in Poland. He added that restoring calm could not mean accepting lawlessness or violence.
“A democratic state has to be strong and capable of enforcing justice,” he said.
The dispute over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal dates back to 2015 , when the governing Civic Platform and opposition Law and Justice parties clashed over the appointment of five judges. It has since developed into a wider conflict over judicial independence, the Tribunal’s composition and the authority of its rulings.
Tusk said his government had tried to resolve the crisis, but its proposals were blocked by PiS and the president, further deepening the dispute.
He said the parliamentary majority then waited for the terms of judges appointed under the previous PiS-led government to expire in an effort to avoid a confrontation.
“We waited calmly for new judges to be chosen, until the terms of their predecessors appointed by PiS expired. The Sejm made its choice, the judges took the oath, but the president did not deign to receive that oath,” Tusk said.
The Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, elected the new judges, who took their oaths of office. Nawrocki did not formally receive the oaths, while Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski refused to allow the new judges to take up their duties.
Tusk described the newly elected judges as legally appointed and said they had been attacked. He also criticised politicians and activists linked to PiS and the far-right Confederation party over their conduct during the confrontation.
He compared the dispute to a thief stealing an elderly woman’s handbag and then accusing others of violence when they try to recover it.
“In certain matters there can be no compromise,” he said, adding that lawlessness could not be negotiated away.
Physical force, aggression and party interests must not determine who is right in a state governed by the rule of law, he added.
Tusk also said no politician, including the president, had the right to enter a court or tribunal, issue instructions to judges or intimidate them. He was referring to Nawrocki’s visit to the Tribunal building after turning his plane around while travelling to Senegal.
Tusk warned that pro-Russian groups could exploit the political conflict.
He pointed to Russian bots operating online which, in his assessment, were supporting opponents of Poland’s current constitutional order.
He said the Constitutional Tribunal would operate in accordance with the constitution and independently of the executive.
As head of government, Tusk pledged to provide the institution with the security and conditions needed to carry out its duties.
“And I intend to fulfil this task,” he said.
However, the speech offered no concrete agreement with Nawrocki or detailed plan to resolve the dispute.

articles.title_orig: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.title_zh: I built an AI Tamagotchi before Meta could
articles.content_orig:
We have Muse Charm at home.
We have Muse Charm at home.
Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta made AI look so stinking cute by giving it a squishy little face — and this holiday season, he wants to sell you a Muse Charm so you can carry your jolly AI helper around like a Tamagotchi.
But I won’t be buying one, because we have Muse Charm at home . It cost just $50, and I’ve decided the learning experience was worth it.
My version doesn’t sport cameras or a 5G cellular radio , but it really talks to Muse and has cute avatars, too! It doubles as a pocket watch and a remote camera viewfinder, and it can (theoretically) control my smart home.
Or at least it can if you inject a lot of extra vibe code.
Weeks ago, I paid $50 to get a 1.75-inch touchscreen computer pendant drop-shipped from China — specifically the Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.75C . Not only does the push-to-talk AI devkit look a lot like the Muse Charm, but it’s officially sanctioned by Meta. It’s one of the company’s first suggestions if you want to build a “Muse Gadget,” a device that uses Meta’s open-source code and tokens to directly connect to its Muse AI cloud.
When the silver metal pocket watch arrived, it felt pretty useless to start. Setup was easy enough — I just plugged it into my PC and pointed Claude at Meta’s GitHub, then paired it to the Muse phone app. But even after I put Meta’s keys on the device, Muse originally thought I was sending it audio clips to transcribe rather than commands. After I cleared that up, Muse’s responses were still slow, and it didn’t answer me out loud. It was hard to tell what it was saying since it only showed a few words onscreen at a time, with no place to read full messages unless I whipped out my phone with its own Muse app.
Meta’s build also only came with a single Jolly avatar that mostly just sat there and looked cute, and it wouldn’t automatically discover smart home gadgets like Amazon Echo or Google Home devices do. (This gadget really didn’t do anything useful after my initial install.) And though Meta AI software engineers Anant Narayanan and Jeremy Payne include a neat sample app showing how Muse Gadgets can stream video from your phone camera, the lack of a remote shutter button made it not so useful for taking photos.
But a few sessions of Claude Code filled in almost all those holes. All I had to do was plug the Waveshare back into my PC, then ask Claude to reprogram each thing I wanted.
When I complained to Claude that I couldn’t properly read or hear Muse’s replies to my asks, issues that others have mentioned as well , Claude built a conversation history page so I can swipe right to read what it said, and I plugged in a British AI voice from ElevenLabs that speaks its answers out loud. (The voice was the least soul-sucking of the ones in ElevenLabs’ free tier, my wife and I agree, even if it doesn’t match the Muse avatars’ cuddly vibe at all.)
Thanks to Claude, I can now press a button to make my phone take a picture from across the room with a high-quality live preview, and my phone’s front-facing camera no longer displays upside down. Claude made fairly short work of adding a low-quality camera preview over Bluetooth, too, so I don’t need to be on home Wi-Fi to get photos from creative angles.
I asked Claude to make a whole batch of different avatars like the ones Meta showed off during Meta Connect, and to add a Tamagotchi-like minigame where they need food, play, sleep, and a bath. When the game seemed too simple to capture any attention, I had it add four different levels of hunger, boredom, and dirt. I decided treats should make a crunchy mess and get avatars dirtier when they eat them, and that too much play should tire out a pet. My wish was Claude’s command.
When I noticed I was accidentally letting go of the push-to-talk button too soon and making Muse choke on almost-empty audio, vibe coding fixed it minutes later by sending only audio over one second in length. The only obvious lag I’m seeing now is from Meta’s own servers — sometimes they’re responsive, sometimes they lag quite a bit.
It was so easy to let Claude reprogram the pendant that I asked it to build a few features specifically for this video in this story, including a working pocket watch face with three hands that actually tells the time. (That took it 15 minutes; now, when I say the hardware looks like a pocket watch, you can see what I mean!) It even found, downloaded, trimmed, and loaded video clips of Zuck introducing the Muse Charm and installed a video player so I could play those clips on the Waveshare.
I want you to understand I have no coding experience, and so I have no idea if any of this code is good. It might be fatally flawed. Nor do I trust Meta or its Muse agent with my email or my home network, particularly after hearing how it leaked one reviewer’s home address . (I put it on guest Wi-Fi from the get-go as a precaution.)
That means I don’t really know how useful a Muse Charm may or may not be for those who do know how to code and are willing to take a bigger leap of faith. But after nearly dropping a bulky little silver pendant a couple of times, one with no more Muse functionality than my phone (and quite a bit less without additional code), I’m thinking Muse itself isn’t the reason to buy a dedicated compute pocket watch.
The reason to have a dedicated piece of hardware is to do things you can’t do on the phone that’s already in your pocket, like coding the entire gadget to do whatever you want. Which makes me wonder: Will the actual Muse Charm be this freely programmable, or would the kind of people who’d buy one be better off with a development kit? I guess we’ll see when it ships.

articles.title_orig: Chipotle is leaning on new menu items to bring diners back
articles.title_zh: Chipotle is leaning on new menu items to bring diners back
articles.content_orig:
For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.
Shares of Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) rose 8.9% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while the S&P 500 fell 0.3%. The gain came a day after Chipotle reported its third-quarter results on October 28. Revenue came in above estimates, while adjusted earnings per share fell below them. Four of the chain’s five peers also posted smaller gains during that session. What in Chipotle’s results did news reports link to the rise?
Chipotle Topped Sales Estimates As Transactions Rose
Chipotle’s third-quarter revenue reached $3,293 million, a little above the $3,287 million analysts expected. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $0.27, below the $0.29 estimate. The company released its results after the market closed on Wednesday. News reports linked Thursday’s rise to same-store sales that topped estimates, as well as to the chain’s push to bring customer traffic back .
During the October 28 call, management said same-store sales increased 2.1% in the quarter and transactions rose 0.8%. It added that Pollo Asado’s return on August 31 brought in extra transactions, while Chili Lime Chips, launched the same day, got more guests to add chips.
Fresh products give buyers a reason to return; an unchanged lineup can stall. Consider Tesla, which got 98% of last quarter’s deliveries from the Model 3 and Model Y and saw deliveries fall two years in a row. Read Trefis Big Story : How Tesla Blundered .
The industry saw a pullback in the first part of October, management said, but Chipotle’s transactions have since turned positive again. Management expects fourth-quarter same-store sales to rise around 2% overall, with the growth rate reaching 3% to 4% by the end of the quarter as smoked brisket returns to the menu in November.
Margins slipped in the quarter. Management put the company’s restaurant-level margin, its own adjusted measure, at 23.3%. That figure is down 120 basis points from a year earlier.
Did Chipotle Rise With Its Restaurant Peers?
Most of Chipotle’s peers also rose, though by much less. Four of the five companies on the Trefis peer list gained during the session, leaving Restaurant Brands International as the only decline. Texas Roadhouse posted the largest advance among them at 4.7%. The consumer discretionary sector fund, XLY, rose 0.8% on a day the S&P 500 fell. Chipotle rose almost twice as much as Texas Roadhouse, so a large part of its gain was its own rather than the group’s.
Where Does Chipotle Stock Stand After The Jump?
A rise this large is rare for Chipotle. One session in the prior 365 days saw a rise at least as big. After the jump, the stock was still down 22.3% over the twelve months to October 29, compared with a 13.3% gain for the S&P 500.
Much of that fall occurred in the last three months. The shares lost 16.0% from July 31 to October 29, while the S&P 500 rose 3.3%. Chipotle closed the session at $31.28. That price sits above the stock’s 52-week closing low of $27.52 set on October 23, 2026, and remains well below the closing high of $40.87 reached on January 23, 2026.
Chipotle is expected to report its fourth-quarter 2026 results in February 2027. Same-store sales growth is the figure to watch in that report.

articles.title_orig: Opposition bloc said weighing direct PM elections to break political deadlock
articles.title_zh: Opposition bloc said weighing direct PM elections to break political deadlock
articles.content_orig:
Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections .
Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
So how could a new government be formed?
Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible.
Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls.
Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that.
On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle.
Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office.
Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged.
Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc.
Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Eisenkot , however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind.
Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers.
But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar.
While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament.
Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first.
Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed.
If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out.
After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition.
If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election.
The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed.
A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years.
